newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope seeks to rally France's indifferent Catholics.
newsitem.headline: Pope seeks to rally France's indifferent Catholics.

text.p: Pope John Paul heads to Paris on Thursday to preside at a Roman Catholic world youth festival amid increasing indifference to the Church in France and controversy over his strict moral teachings.
The 77-year-old Pontiff is expected to use his sixth trip to France to focus on social justice and to urge the young to shun material temptations and live more wholesome, spiritual lives.
But he has been loudly criticised by family planning groups and a party in France's leftist government over plans to pay a private visit to the grave of a staunch anti-abortion campaigner.

French Protestants are also upset that the climax of the four-day visit, a mass the Church hopes will draw half a million people, falls on the anniversary of the St Bartholemew's Day massacre of up to 70,000 Huguenots by Catholic forces in 1572.

France is mobilising 7,000 police, soldiers and anti-terrorist commandos for the August 21-24 trip to Paris and the nearby town of Evry after a crude bomb was planted at a basilica ahead of his last visit in September 1996.
Church officials admit that turnout for its World Youth Day celebrations could be embarrassingly below target.
The Church had hoped that 600,000 "young people" -- whom it defines as aged between 17 and 35 -- would flock to France.
It admitted last week that far fewer than forecast had signed up to attend the celebrations, fewer families had come forward to host them and fund-raising had also been a problem.

But the chief organiser, Bishop Michel Dubost, was upbeat on Monday, saying many French pilgrims had registered late. He told reporters 160 countries would be represented, and the number of pilgrims would easily reach 350,000.

A low attendance would again turn the spotlight on how well the Pope can rally the faithful and overcome what he himself identified on his trip last year as a "climate of indifference" weakening religious following in once fervently Catholic France.
Of France's nearly 50 million Catholics, only six million attend mass regularly and many ignore or oppose bans on abortion, contraception and homosexuality.

The Pope's plans to visit the grave of his friend Jerome Lejeune, a genetic scientist and outspoken anti-abortion campaigner, on August 22, have been branded a "provocation" by the Radical Socialist Party (PRS), a partner in the government.

The PRS urged the Pontiff to cancel the plan and rebel "red" bishop Jacques Gaillot, ousted by the Vatican from his diocese in 1995 because of his liberal views, called it a "blessing for anti-abortion commandos", increasingly militant in France.
The Pope, who had surgery last year to remove his appendix but has appeared relatively well recently, will begin his visit by meeting President Jacques Chirac at the Elysee Palace.
On Friday he will beatify Frederick Ozanam, a 19th century professor at the Sorbonne who was committed to social justice.
Protestant groups have blasted the timing of the final mass on August 24 as "inopportune" and want a gesture of remembrance to mark the St Bartholemew's Day killings four centuries ago.
But Protestant clergymen have played down the coincidence of dates and Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, himself a Protestant, plans to see the Pope off at Orly airport later that day.
The four-day visit -- the Pope's 79th foreign trip -- will be another test of his health in a demanding year for overseas travel.
He has visited Bosnia, the Czech Republic, Lebanon and Poland this year and goes to Brazil in October. He is due to make an historic trip to Cuba in January.
